column3: With nobody clearly in charge at Ásaker, those who keep order are unsure whose orders to follow, and petty crime has risen in the gap.
This is how Ásaker looks on a first visit; a season there might show it differently.
The village has never needed to think about what is outside it, and does not.
The village's plan for an army is to not be interesting to one, and everybody here can state the plan.
Ásaker keeps no court and no gaol, and no wrong done there is written down; order is kept by whoever is armed and standing there, and when they leave, nothing keeps it.
Ásaker's pay book is always behind: its defenders are paid late or not at all, and people owed wages are slow to turn out when trouble comes.
You can walk into Ásaker from any direction and pass nobody on the way in.
Ásaker has no organized force. Defense here is individual armed citizens, with no command, no training and no way to coordinate a response.
Ásaker keeps no defence against anything it cannot see.
Ásaker has not been attacked lately, and if it were, it would struggle to hold.
Several people at Ásaker could order the defence and none can do it alone, so they watch each other instead of the roads.
Ásaker should come through this crisis if nothing else goes wrong, though its defence has had to change to meet it.
Ásaker is too small to wall and knows it; the village's safety is its neighbours, its distance, and its unimportance.
What goes wrong at Ásaker goes wrong one thing at a time and belongs to whoever did it.
No criminal's money appears in the Priestly Guidance's accounts at Ásaker, so what the hall spends is spent on the village.
